Eggs of the White-faced storm petrel (Pelagodroma marina) are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature that facilitates embryonic development over a relatively protracted incubation period of 50 days [ab = 50 days]. Newly hatched chicks, emerging from this calcareous egg, are altricial and weigh approximately 6.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 6.5 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the substantial energetic investment required for the parents to provision a single offspring through the subsequent nestling phase. Given the challenges of foraging far out at sea, this chick mass is typical of small Procellariiformes. The yolk-dependent embryo relies entirely on its endogenous reserves until hatching, after which the transition to parental provisioning begins immediately. The incubating adult maintains a remarkably consistent egg temperature, a commitment that requires the non-breeding partner to undertake long-distance foraging trips to replenish its own body condition before taking over incubation duties. This biparental care strategy is essential for the successful development of the altricial nestling.

Under the thermal conditions characterizing the active metabolic period of this pelagic seabird (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), the chick undergoes a critical developmental milestone known as fledging. The time since birth at fledging for the White-faced storm petrel is 68 days [tx = 68 days], a duration during which the chick progresses from a downy, pin-feathered nestling entirely dependent on its parents to a flight-feather-matured fledgling capable of sustained flight at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This period of intense growth and feather development is energetically demanding, and the chick accumulates substantial lipid reserves to support its first days of independence at sea. Following nest departure, the fledgling quickly transitions to exogenous feeding, mastering first prey capture as it disperses from the breeding colony. The achievement of this developmental stage marks the end of parental provisioning and the onset of the juvenile phase. The duration of the nestling period is a key life-history variable that correlates strongly with adult body size and foraging ecology across the Procellariiformes.

Following the achievement of flight, the juvenile White-faced storm petrel enters a prolonged sub-adult phase. Under the same thermal regime of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], reproductive maturation proceeds slowly, with the time since birth at puberty estimated at 204 days [tp = 204 days]. This relatively late onset of gonadal maturation compared to other small seabirds reflects the energetic constraints of attaining a body condition sufficient for breeding in a resource-poor pelagic environment. The immature individual must develop not only its reproductive organs but also the foraging proficiency required to sustain both itself and a future chick. This pre-reproductive juvenile period is characterized by extensive prospecting behavior at colonies and long-distance oceanic movements that likely contribute to learning migration routes and foraging grounds. The duration of this stage is a critical determinant of the overall generation time of the population. Sexual maturation involves a complex interplay of hormonal changes and body condition thresholds.

The White-faced storm petrel does not begin breeding immediately upon reaching puberty. Instead, individuals typically defer their first reproduction until they have accumulated sufficient experience and energy reserves. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 2 years [tR = approximately 2 years], a delay that allows young birds to refine their foraging skills and establish a nesting territory within a crowded colony at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. A single egg is laid per nesting attempt [N_R_i = single egg is laid per nesting attempt], and each breeding season, a pair typically makes one such nesting attempt [F_R_i = breeding season, a pair typically makes one such nesting attempt], reflecting the maximum reproductive rate characteristic of this long-lived species. This low annual fecundity is offset by sustained adult survival. The first successful breeding event is a significant demographic milestone that marks the transition from the pre-reproductive juvenile stage to the breeding adult bird stage. The adult then faces the considerable energetic challenge of provisioning a single chick over many weeks, a task that requires both parents to forage intensively.

Adults of this species are remarkably long-lived. Under the active metabolic temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the maximum lifespan for the White-faced storm petrel has been recorded at 30 years [am = 30 years], with some individuals known to survive for at least 16 years based on banding studies. This extended lifespan, characteristic of many Procellariiformes, is a life-history strategy that compensates for the extremely low annual fecundity of a single egg per year. The ultimate wet weight of a fully-grown adult, about 60 grams [Wwi = about 60 grams], is a modest body mass for a bird that undertakes prodigious trans-oceanic migrations. Achieving and maintaining this adult body mass is critical for successful reproduction, as body condition directly influences the ability to produce a single, large, energy-rich egg. The breeding adult bird will often make foraging trips of several thousand kilometers to locate patchily distributed prey before returning to the incubating chick. The species' demography is therefore driven by high adult survival and a low, but consistent, reproductive output.
